content: 1. Clarithromycin should not be used during pregnancy unless there are no suitable alternative therapies. If a patient becomes pregnant while taking this medication, they should be informed of the potential risks to the fetus. Studies in animals, including monkeys, rats, mice, and rabbits, have shown adverse effects on pregnancy outcomes and embryo-fetal development at doses that result in plasma levels 2 to 17 times higher than those achieved in humans at the maximum recommended dose. 2. Hepatic dysfunction, including elevated liver enzymes, hepatocellular damage, and/or cholestatic hepatitis (with or without jaundice), has been reported with clarithromycin use. While this liver dysfunction is typically reversible, severe cases, including fatal hepatic failure, have been reported, often in patients with serious underlying conditions or those taking other medications. Symptoms of hepatitis may include anorexia, jaundice, dark urine, pruritus, or abdominal tenderness. If signs or symptoms of hepatitis occur, clarithromycin should be discontinued immediately. 3. Clarithromycin has been associated with QT interval prolongation and, in rare cases, arrhythmias, including torsades de pointes. Fatalities have been reported. Clarithromycin should be avoided in patients with ongoing proarrhythmic conditions, such as uncorrected hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia, significant bradycardia, or those taking Class IA (e.g., quinidine, procainamide) or Class III (e.g., dofetilide, amiodarone, sotalol) antiarrhythmic agents. Elderly patients may be more susceptible to these effects. 4. Serious adverse reactions have been reported in patients taking clarithromycin concurrently with CYP3A4 substrates, such as verapamil, amlodipine, or diltiazem. Clarithromycin should be used cautiously with medications that induce the CYP3A4 enzyme. 5. Life-threatening and fatal drug interactions have been reported in patients treated with clarithromycin and colchicine. Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor, and this interaction can occur even at recommended doses. If co-administration is necessary in patients with normal renal and hepatic function, the colchicine dose should be reduced, and patients should be monitored for signs of colchicine toxicity. Co-administration is contraindicated in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. 6. Increased sedation and prolonged sedation have been reported with the concurrent use of clarithromycin and triazolobenzodiazepines, such as triazolam and midazolam. 7. The concurrent use of clarithromycin with oral hypoglycemic agents or insulin can result in significant hypoglycemia. With certain hypoglycemic drugs, such as nateglinide, pioglitazone, repaglinide, and rosiglitazone, CYP3A enzyme inhibition by clarithromycin may contribute to hypoglycemia. Careful glucose monitoring is recommended. 8. Co-administration of clarithromycin with warfarin increases the risk of serious bleeding and significant elevations in INR and prothrombin time. INR and prothrombin times should be frequently monitored during concurrent use. 9. The use of clarithromycin with lovastatin or simvastatin is contraindicated because these statins are extensively metabolized by CYP3A4, and clarithromycin increases their plasma concentrations, raising the risk of myopathy, including rhabdomyolysis. Cases of rhabdomyolysis have been reported. If clarithromycin treatment cannot be avoided, therapy with lovastatin or simvastatin must be suspended during the course of treatment. If co-administration with atorvastatin or pravastatin is unavoidable, the atorvastatin dose should not exceed 20 mg daily, and the pravastatin dose should not exceed 40 mg daily. The lowest effective statin dose should be prescribed. 10. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including clarithromycin, and may range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Antibacterial treatment alters the normal flora of the colon, leading to C. difficile overgrowth. C. difficile produces toxins A and B, which contribute to CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile can cause increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be refractory to antimicrobial therapy and may require colectomy. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use, even up to two months after administration. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued. Appropriate fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, antibiotic treatment of C. difficile, and surgical evaluation should be initiated as clinically indicated. 11. Severe acute hypersensitivity reactions, such as anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), and Henoch-Schönlein purpura, require immediate discontinuation of clarithromycin therapy and urgent initiation of appropriate treatment. 12. For combination therapy with other drugs, refer to the warnings section of the package inserts for those medications. 13. Clarithromycin should not be prescribed in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or a prophylactic indication, as this increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Clarithromycin is primarily excreted via the liver and kidneys. No dosage adjustment is needed for patients with hepatic impairment and normal renal function. However, in cases of severe renal impairment, with or without coexisting hepatic impairment, dosage reduction or prolonged dosing intervals may be necessary. Clarithromycin in combination with ranitidine bismuth citrate is not recommended in patients with creatinine clearance less than 25 mL/min or in those with a history of acute porphyria. Exacerbation of myasthenia gravis symptoms and new-onset myasthenic syndrome symptoms have been reported with clarithromycin therapy. 14. Patients should be counseled that antibacterial drugs, including clarithromycin, should only be used to treat bacterial infections and not viral infections (e.g., the common cold). Patients should be advised to take the medication exactly as directed, even if they feel better early in the course of therapy. Skipping doses or not completing the full course of therapy may reduce the effectiveness of treatment and increase the likelihood of bacterial resistance. Diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics and usually resolves when the antibiotic is discontinued. However, if watery and bloody stools occur (with or without stomach cramps and fever) even two or more months after the last dose, patients should contact their physician immediately. Clarithromycin may interact with other drugs, so patients should inform their doctor of any other medications they are taking. Clarithromycin tablets and oral suspension can be taken with or without food and with milk, but clarithromycin XL tablets should be taken with food. The suspension should not be refrigerated.
